claim: Erastin is a potent, selective inhibitor of system xc−.
source: In this study, we report that the small molecule erastin is a potent, selective inhibitor of system xc−.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including radioactive uptake assays and glutamate release assays.

claim: Inhibition of cystine–glutamate exchange leads to activation of an ER stress response.
source: RNA sequencing revealed that inhibition of cystine–glutamate exchange leads to activation of an ER stress response and upregulation of CHAC1, providing a pharmacodynamic marker for system xc− inhibition.
evidence: RNA sequencing data and subsequent validation experiments demonstrate upregulation of ER stress response genes.

claim: CHAC1 upregulation provides a pharmacodynamic marker for system xc− inhibition.
source: RNA sequencing revealed that inhibition of cystine–glutamate exchange leads to activation of an ER stress response and upregulation of CHAC1, providing a pharmacodynamic marker for system xc− inhibition.
evidence: RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR data show CHAC1 is the most highly upregulated gene in response to erastin treatment.

claim: Sorafenib inhibits system xc− function.
source: We also found that the clinically approved anti-cancer drug sorafenib, but not other kinase inhibitors, inhibits system xc− function and can trigger ER stress and ferroptosis.
evidence: Glutamate release assays and other functional assays demonstrate sorafenib's ability to inhibit system xc−.

claim: Sorafenib can trigger ER stress and ferroptosis.
source: We also found that the clinically approved anti-cancer drug sorafenib, but not other kinase inhibitors, inhibits system xc− function and can trigger ER stress and ferroptosis.
evidence: Cell viability assays with ferroptosis inhibitors, ER stress markers, and glutathione depletion assays support this claim.

claim: Patients treated with sorafenib exhibited unique metabolic and phenotypic alterations compared to patients treated with other kinase-inhibiting drugs.
source: In an analysis of hospital records and adverse event reports, we found that patients treated with sorafenib exhibited unique metabolic and phenotypic alterations compared to patients treated with other kinase-inhibiting drugs.
evidence: Analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) data shows distinct patterns of adverse events for sorafenib.

claim: System xc− is a cell-surface Na+-independent cystine–glutamate antiporter composed of SLC7A11 (xCT) and SLC3A2 (4F2hc).
source: System xc− is a cell-surface Na+-independent cystine–glutamate antiporter composed of the 12-pass transmembrane transporter protein SLC7A11 (xCT) linked via a disulfide bridge to the single-pass transmembrane regulatory subunit SLC3A2 (4F2hc) (Sato et al., 1999; Conrad and Sato, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the structure of system xc−.

claim: System xc− is required for normal mammalian blood plasma redox homeostasis, skin pigmentation, immune system function, and memory formation.
source: System xc− is required for normal mammalian blood plasma redox homeostasis, skin pigmentation, immune system function, and memory formation (Chintala et al., 2005; Sato et al., 2005; De Bundel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Aberrant system xc− function is implicated in tumor growth and survival, cancer stem cell maintenance, drug resistance, and neurological dysfunction.
source: Aberrant system xc− function is implicated in tumor growth and survival, cancer stem cell maintenance, drug resistance, and neurological dysfunction (Okuno et al., 2003; Buckingham et al., 2011; Ishimoto et al., 2011; Yae et al., 2012; Timmerman et al., 2013)
evidence: Multiple citations support the role of system xc− in various pathological conditions.

claim: Sulfasalazine (SAS) is a low potency, metabolically unstable small molecule that modulates system xc− activity.
source: Efforts to treat gliomas and lymphomas in human patients by modulating system xc− activity with the low potency, metabolically unstable small molecule, sulfasalazine (SAS, Gout et al., 2001), were unsuccessful (Robe et al., 2009).
evidence: This characterization is supported by citations to clinical trials and previous research.

claim: Erastin prevents Na+-independent cystine uptake.
source: We previously demonstrated that the small molecule erastin prevents Na+-independent cystine uptake (Dixon et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of intracellular soluble and lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of intracellular soluble and lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS), a process that is counteracted by the glutathione-dependent activity of the enzyme glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) (Dixon and Stockwell, 2013; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research defining ferroptosis.

claim: Erastin-induced death is rescued by iron chelator ciclopirox olamine (CPX), lipophilic antioxidants trolox and ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), MEK inhibitor U0126, protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), and reducing agent beta-mercaptoethanol (β-ME).
source: We observed that in five different human cancer cell lines, cell death induced by either erastin or SAS was rescued by the same canonical ferroptosis inhibitors: the iron chelator ciclopirox olamine (CPX), the lipophilic antioxidants trolox and ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), the MEK inhibitor U0126, the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) and the reducing agent beta-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) (Dixon et al., 2012; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Modulatory profiling data shown in Figure 1A,B demonstrates rescue of erastin-induced death by these compounds.

claim: SAS-induced death is rescued by the same canonical ferroptosis inhibitors as erastin-induced death.
source: We observed that in five different human cancer cell lines, cell death induced by either erastin or SAS was rescued by the same canonical ferroptosis inhibitors: the iron chelator ciclopirox olamine (CPX), the lipophilic antioxidants trolox and ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), the MEK inhibitor U0126, the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) and the reducing agent beta-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) (Dixon et al., 2012; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Modulatory profiling data shown in Figure 1A,B demonstrates rescue of SAS-induced death by these compounds.

claim: The inhibition of cell death by β-ME indicates that cell death most likely involves inhibition of system xc− function.
source: The inhibition of cell death by β-ME indicates that cell death most likely involves inhibition of system xc− function, as β-ME treatment can generate mixed disulfides taken up by other transporters, thereby circumventing the need for system xc− function (Ishii et al., 1981).
evidence: This inference is supported by a citation explaining the mechanism of β-ME action and experimental data showing β-ME rescue.

claim: Erastin triggers ferroptosis in multicellular tumor spheroids (MCTSs).
source: We observed that HT-1080 and Calu-1 MCTSs were killed by erastin and RSL3 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: MCTS viability data shown in Figure 1C,D demonstrates erastin-induced death in 3D culture.

claim: The effects of erastin on MCTSs are rescued by Fer-1.
source: The effects of both erastin and RSL3 were rescued by Fer-1, while β-ME suppressed the lethality of erastin, but not of RSL3, as expected (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: MCTS viability data shown in Figure 1C,D demonstrates Fer-1 rescue of erastin effects.

claim: β-ME suppresses the lethality of erastin but not RSL3 in MCTSs.
source: The effects of both erastin and RSL3 were rescued by Fer-1, while β-ME suppressed the lethality of erastin, but not of RSL3, as expected (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: MCTS viability data shown in Figure 1C,D demonstrates selective β-ME rescue of erastin but not RSL3.

claim: Erastin triggers ferroptosis under both high (21%) and low (1%) oxygen conditions.
source: We observed that compared to DMSO-treated cells, erastin (5 μM)-treated cells were killed under both high and low O2 conditions with little (DU-145) or no (HT-1080) difference in lethality (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Cell viability data under different oxygen conditions shown in Figure 1E,F demonstrates erastin lethality at both oxygen levels.

claim: Erastin-induced death under both high and low oxygen conditions is suppressed by Fer-1 and CPX.
source: In both cell lines, erastin-induced death was suppressed by both Fer-1 (1 μM) and CPX (5 μM) (Figure 1E,F), indicating that the same lethal mechanism (i.e., ferroptosis) was responsible for cell death under both high and low O2 conditions.
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 1E,F demonstrates rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors under both oxygen conditions.

claim: Erastin treatment (5 μM) completely abolished Na+-independent uptake of [14C]-cystine in HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells.
source: Erastin treatment (5 μM) completely abolished the Na+-independent uptake of radiolabelled [14C]-cystine in both HT-1080 fibrosarcoma and Calu-1 lung carcinoma cancer cells, as did sulfasalazine (SAS) at 100-fold higher concentrations (500 μM) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrates complete inhibition of cystine uptake by erastin.

claim: SAS at 500 μM completely abolished Na+-independent uptake of [14C]-cystine in HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells.
source: Erastin treatment (5 μM) completely abolished the Na+-independent uptake of radiolabelled [14C]-cystine in both HT-1080 fibrosarcoma and Calu-1 lung carcinoma cancer cells, as did sulfasalazine (SAS) at 100-fold higher concentrations (500 μM) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrates complete inhibition of cystine uptake by SAS.

claim: Erastin and SAS have no effect on Na+-independent [14C]-phenylalanine uptake.
source: Conversely, erastin and SAS had no effect on Na+-independent [14C]-phenylalanine uptake (Figure 2B).
evidence: Radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 2B demonstrates no inhibition of phenylalanine uptake.

claim: Erastin and SAS block system xc− (SLC7A11 + SLC3A2)-mediated cystine uptake selectively over system-L-(SLC7A5 + SLC3A2)-mediated Phe uptake.
source: Thus, in HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells, erastin and SAS block system xc− (SLC7A11 + SLC3A2)-mediated cystine uptake selectivity over other transport systems and amino acids, such as system-L-(SLC7A5 + SLC3A2)-mediated Phe uptake.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential effects on cystine vs phenylalanine uptake shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Erastin inhibits glutamate release in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We confirmed the ability of erastin and SAS to inhibit system xc− using an enzyme-coupled fluorescent assay that detects glutamate release into Na+-containing culture medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 2D,H demonstrates dose-dependent inhibition.

claim: Erastin-A8, a non-lethal erastin analog, does not inhibit glutamate release.
source: First, we showed that erastin (1) inhibited glutamate release, while a non-lethal (Yagoda et al., 2007) erastin analog lacking the p-chlorophenoxy moiety (erastin-A8, 2) did not (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 2D demonstrates lack of inhibition by erastin-A8.

claim: Silencing of SLC7A11 with siRNAs results in significant inhibition of glutamate release.
source: Second, we showed that both erastin treatment and silencing of SLC7A11 with either of two independent siRNAs resulted in a significant, quantitatively similar inhibition of glutamate release (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: Glutamate release assay data with siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 2E,F demonstrates inhibition.

claim: Silencing of SLC7A5 has no effect on basal or erastin-mediated inhibition of glutamate release.
source: silencing of the system L transporter subunit SLC7A5 using two independent siRNAs had no effect on basal or erastin-mediated inhibition of glutamate release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data with SLC7A5 knockdown shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C demonstrates no effect.

claim: RSL3, artesunate and PEITC do not inhibit glutamate release.
source: Third, we found that only erastin and SAS inhibited glutamate release, while, as expected, RSL3, artesunate and PEITC did not; while artesunate and PEITC induce iron-dependent cell death, neither are known to inhibit system xc− or induce ferroptosis (Trachootham et al., 2006; Hamacher-Brady et al., 2011; Dixon et al., 2012; Figure 2G).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 2G demonstrates no inhibition by these compounds.

claim: Erastin is approximately 2500 times more potent than SAS as an inhibitor of system xc− function in HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells.
source: Using the glutamate release assay to quantify inhibition of system xc− activity, we found that erastin was ∼2500 times more potent than SAS as an inhibitor of system xc− function in both HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells (HT-1080: erastin IC50 = 0.20 µM, 95% C.I. 0.11–0.34 µM, SAS IC50 = 450 µM, 95% C.I. 280–710 µM; Calu-1: erastin IC50 = 0.14 µM, 95% C.I. 0.081–0.21 µM, SAS IC50 = 460 µM, 95% C.I. 350–590 µM) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Dose-response data for glutamate release inhibition shown in Figure 2H with calculated IC50 values.

claim: The lethal potency of erastin analogs in HT-1080 cells correlates significantly with the degree of system xc− inhibition in CCF-STTG1 cells (Pearson R2 = 0.86, p<0.0001).
source: Overall, the lethal potency in HT-1080 cells was found to correlate significantly with the degree of system xc− inhibition observed in CCF-STTG1 cells (Pearson R2 = 0.86, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of data from erastin analog testing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Modifications to the quinazolinone core (Region A) of erastin result in moderate to severe losses of lethal potency.
source: Modifications to this region (4–10), including substitution of the quinazolinone for quinolone (4) or indole (5), obtained using a Meth-Cohn quinoline synthesis (Supplementary file 1), resulted in moderate to severe losses of lethal potency compared to 3, suggesting that the quinazolinone core scaffold is essential for the lethality of erastin.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates reduced potency of these analogs.

claim: Modifications to the piperazine linker (Region B) of erastin are not tolerated.
source: Modifications to the piperazine linker (Region B, 11–12) were not tolerated, with 12 being completely inactive in both the HT-1080 lethality and CCF-STTG1 glutamate release assays.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates loss of activity for these analogs.

claim: Single atom changes to the acetoxy spacer (Region C) of erastin are poorly tolerated.
source: Single atom changes to the acetoxy spacer (Region C, 13–15) were likewise poorly tolerated, resulting in significant losses in potency that correlated with reduced inhibition of system xc− activity.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates reduced potency for these analogs.

claim: The chlorine atom in Region D of erastin may make a key halogen bonding interaction essential for binding.
source: As suggested by the weakened potency of 16 and 17, and the inactivity of 18, the chlorine atom may make a key halogen bonding interaction with the surrounding environment (Wilcken et al., 2012) that is essential for binding.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 3B and citation to halogen bonding literature support this inference.

claim: Modifications to Region E of erastin, including addition of bromo, phenyl, or furanyl substituents, result in fivefold or greater improvements in lethal potency.
source: Finally, modifications to Region E, including addition of a bromo group (20), a phenyl (21) or a furanyl substituent (22) resulted in fivefold or greater improvements in lethal potency that were mirrored by fivefold to 10-fold improvements in the inhibition of system xc− activity compared to 3
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates improved potency for these analogs.

claim: Compound 21 inhibits glutamate release with below 5 nM potency in the CCF-STTG1 assay.
source: the most potent compound, 21, inhibited glutamate release with below 5 nM potency in the CCF-STTG1 assay.
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates sub-5 nM IC50 for compound 21.

claim: Erastin analogs 21 and 3 retain selectivity towards BJeLR vs BJeH cells.
source: We tested the most potent lethal analog (21), along with the parent compound (3) and a representative non-lethal analog (14), in these cell lines. While 14 was inactive, we found that both lethal analogs (21 and 3) retained selectivity towards BJeLR vs BJeH cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 3C demonstrates selective lethality in oncogenic RAS-expressing cells.

claim: Compound 21 is more than 20-fold more potent than compound 3 in BJeLR cells.
source: Consistent with the pattern of lethality observed in HT-1080 cells, 21 was a more than 20-fold more potent lethal molecule compared to 3 (BJeLR EC50 of 22 nM [95% C.I. 20-25 nM] vs 490 nM [95% C.I. 350-690 nM], respectively).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 3C with calculated EC50 values demonstrates improved potency.

claim: Co-treatment with β-ME reverses all erastin-induced changes in mRNA expression.
source: In support of the hypothesis, erastin-induced changes in mRNA expression were reversed by co-treatment with β-ME for all 33 up-regulated genes (Mann–Whitney test, p<0.0001) and for each of the four down-regulated genes.
evidence: RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4A,B demonstrates reversal of gene expression changes by β-ME.

claim: The effects of erastin on cellular physiology detectable at the level of mRNA expression are due to depletion of intracellular cystine.
source: These results suggest that the effects of erastin on cellular physiology detectable at the level of mRNA expression are due to depletion of intracellular cystine, arising as a consequence of inhibition of system xc− function.
evidence: This inference is based on the complete reversal of gene expression changes by β-ME, which bypasses system xc−.

claim: Genes upregulated by erastin are significantly enriched for GO Biological Process terms related to ER stress and unfolded protein responses.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that the 33 up-regulated genes were significantly enriched for GO Biological Process terms related directly to the ER stress and unfolded protein responses (GO:0034976, response to endoplasmic reticulum stress, p=8.0 e−11; GO:0006987, activation of signaling protein activity involved in unfolded protein response, p=1.3 e−9; GO:0032075, positive regulation of nuclease activity, p=1.5 e−9).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data demonstrates significant enrichment for ER stress terms.

claim: Erastin treatment results in phosphorylation of eIF2alpha and up-regulation of ATF4 at the protein level.
source: We investigated further the connection between erastin treatment and activation of the eIF2alpha-ATF4 pathway and observed that, relative to DMSO-treated controls, erastin treatment (5 μM, 7 hr) resulted in phosphorylation of eIF2alpha and up-regulation of ATF4 at the protein level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A demonstrates increased phospho-eIF2alpha and ATF4 levels.

claim: Erastin treatment does not result in enhanced splicing of XBP1 mRNA.
source: We saw no evidence for enhanced splicing of the XBP1 mRNA, which provides a readout for activation of a parallel ER stress response pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: XBP1 splicing assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B demonstrates no change in splicing.

claim: Co-treatment with actinomycin D delays but does not prevent erastin-induced cell death.
source: In HT-1080 cells, co-treatment with the transcriptional inhibitor actinomycin D (1 μg/ml) inhibited erastin-induced changes in gene expression (see below) and delayed but did not prevent erastin-induced cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C demonstrates delayed but not prevented death.

claim: The transcriptional response to erastin is not essential for the lethality observed following erastin treatment.
source: Thus, while blockade of system xc− by erastin (and other agents, see below) can trigger a robust transcriptional signature indicative of ER stress, it is doubtful that this transcriptional response is essential for the lethality observed following erastin treatment.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that actinomycin D delays but does not prevent erastin-induced death.

claim: CHAC1 is the most highly up-regulated gene in erastin-treated HT-1080 cells by RNA-Seq (approximately 24-fold).
source: We therefore explored the RNA-Seq profiles for suitable candidate PD makers; the most highly up-regulated gene observed in erastin-treated HT-1080 cells by RNA-Seq was CHAC1 (∼24-fold, Figure 4A)
evidence: RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4A demonstrates 24-fold upregulation of CHAC1.

claim: CHAC1 is an ER stress-responsive gene known to be upregulated downstream of ATF4.
source: the most highly up-regulated gene observed in erastin-treated HT-1080 cells by RNA-Seq was CHAC1 (∼24-fold, Figure 4A), an ER stress-responsive gene known to be upregulated downstream of ATF4 (Gargalovic et al., 2006; Mungrue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on CHAC1 regulation.

claim: CHAC1 up-regulation by erastin is fully reversible by co-treatment with β-ME.
source: We validated these results by RT-qPCR using fresh samples prepared from HT-1080 and Calu-1 cells, and confirmed that CHAC1 up-regulation was fully reversible by co-treatment with β-ME (Figure 4C).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C demonstrates reversal of CHAC1 upregulation by β-ME.

claim: Treatment with system xc− inhibitors (erastin and SAS), but not RSL3, artesunate, rotenone or BSO, results in transcriptional upregulation of CHAC1.
source: We examined the specificity of the above response—we observed transcriptional upregulation of CHAC1 following treatment with system xc− inhibitors (erastin and SAS), but not in response to RSL3, artesunate, rotenone or buthionine sulfoximine (BSO), agents that induce oxidative stress, but that do not inhibit system xc− (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D demonstrates selective CHAC1 upregulation by system xc− inhibitors.

claim: CHAC1 upregulation can specifically indicate agents that inhibit system xc− function vs those that trigger redox stress by other means.
source: suggesting that CHAC1 upregulation can specifically indicate agents that inhibit system xc− function vs those that trigger redox stress by other means.
evidence: This inference is based on the selective upregulation of CHAC1 by system xc− inhibitors but not other oxidative stress inducers.

claim: Upregulation of CHAC1 in erastin-treated HT-1080 cells is prevented by co-treatment with actinomycin D or cycloheximide.
source: Upregulation of CHAC1 in erastin-treated HT-1080 cells was prevented by co-treatment with the transcriptional inhibitor actinomycin D as well as the protein synthesis inhibitor CHX, suggesting that CHAC1 mRNA upregulation downstream of erastin treatment requires new transcription and translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D demonstrates prevention of CHAC1 upregulation by these inhibitors.

claim: Across a panel of 13 cancer cell lines, treatment with erastin, but not STS, results in a significant increase in CHAC1 expression.
source: We next tested the generality of CHAC1 upregulation in response to erastin, and observed that across a panel of 13 cancer cell lines, treatment with erastin, but not the apoptosis-inducer STS, resulted in a significant increase in CHAC1 expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E demonstrates CHAC1 upregulation across multiple cell lines.

claim: Sorafenib synergizes with erastin or BSO treatment in A549 and HCT-116 cells.
source: Overall, we observed that the modulatory effect (Me) values for the test compounds clustered around zero (i.e., additive enhancement of death), with the exception of RSL3, phenylarsine oxide (PAO) and sorafenib (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Modulatory profiling data shown in Figure 5A,B demonstrates synergistic effects (Me > 0) for sorafenib.

claim: Sorafenib (10 μM, 24 hr) treatment-induced cell death in HT-1080 cells is significantly inhibited by β-ME, Fer-1 and DFO.
source: First, we found that in HT-1080 cells sorafenib (10 μM, 24 hr) treatment-induced cell death was significantly inhibited by the known small molecule ferroptosis suppressors β-ME, Fer-1 and DFO (Dixon et al., 2012); these same inhibitors suppress erastin (10 μM, 24 hr)-induced ferroptotic death, but not STS-induced apoptotic death (Figure 5C).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 5C demonstrates rescue of sorafenib-induced death by ferroptosis inhibitors.

claim: Sorafenib alone can trigger ferroptosis.
source: Thus, sorafenib alone can trigger ferroptosis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the rescue of sorafenib-induced death by ferroptosis-specific inhibitors.

claim: Sorafenib results in a dose-dependent inhibition of system xc− function in HT-1080 cells.
source: Indeed, we observed that sorafenib, like erastin, but not the kinase inhibitor imatinib, resulted in a dose-dependent inhibition of system xc− function, as assessed using the glutamate release assay in HT-1080 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 5D demonstrates dose-dependent inhibition by sorafenib.

claim: The ability of sorafenib and erastin to suppress system xc− activity is not inhibited by co-treatment with Fer-1.
source: The ability of sorafenib and erastin to suppress system xc− activity was not inhibited by co-treatment with Fer-1, demonstrating that this effect is upstream of Fer-1-sensitive ROS accumulation (Figure 5D), as expected.
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 5D demonstrates no effect of Fer-1 on system xc− inhibition.

claim: Sorafenib treatment causes robust transcriptional upregulation of CHAC1 in HT-1080 cells.
source: Likewise, similar to erastin and SAS, we observed a robust transcriptional upregulation of CHAC1 in HT-1080 cells in response to sorafenib treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D demonstrates CHAC1 upregulation by sorafenib.

claim: Sorafenib treatment causes upregulation of biochemical markers of ER stress (phosphorylation of eIF2alpha and increased levels of ATF4) without change in XBP1 splicing.
source: We also observed upregulation of the same biochemical markers of ER stress observed previously with erastin, namely phosphorylation of eIF2alpha and increased levels of ATF4, without any change in XBP1 splicing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Western blot and XBP1 splicing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B demonstrates ER stress markers.

claim: Sorafenib treatment (10 μM, 18 hr) of HT-1080 cells significantly depletes total glutathione.
source: Finally, as observed previously with erastin treatment (Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014), we found that sorafenib treatment (10 μM, 18 hr) of HT-1080 cells significantly depleted total glutathione and resulted in the accumulation of lipid peroxides as detected by flow cytometry using C11-BODIPY 581/591 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Glutathione assay data shown in Figure 5E demonstrates depletion by sorafenib.

claim: Sorafenib treatment (10 μM, 18 hr) of HT-1080 cells results in the accumulation of lipid peroxides.
source: Finally, as observed previously with erastin treatment (Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014), we found that sorafenib treatment (10 μM, 18 hr) of HT-1080 cells significantly depleted total glutathione and resulted in the accumulation of lipid peroxides as detected by flow cytometry using C11-BODIPY 581/591 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: C11-BODIPY flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F demonstrates lipid peroxide accumulation.

claim: Sorafenib inhibits system xc−-mediated cystine import, leading to ER stress, glutathione depletion and the iron-dependent accumulation of lipid ROS.
source: Together, these results suggest that, like erastin, sorafenib inhibits system xc−-mediated cystine import, leading to ER stress, glutathione depletion and the iron-dependent accumulation of lipid ROS.
evidence: This conclusion integrates multiple experimental observations about sorafenib's effects.

claim: In all five cell lines examined, sorafenib and erastin treatments (20 μM) cause comparable inhibition of system xc− function.
source: Consistent with the initial results, in all five cell lines examined, we observed that sorafenib and erastin treatments (20 μM) caused a comparable inhibition of system xc− function, as assessed by glutamate release (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrates comparable inhibition.

claim: Sorafenib triggers Fer-1-suppressible ferroptosis in HT-1080 cells only within a narrow concentration window.
source: However, unlike erastin, we observed that sorafenib triggered Fer-1-suppressible ferroptosis in HT-1080 cells only within a narrow concentration window (sorafenib EC50 = 18 μM, sorafenib+Fer-1 EC50 = 43 μM), before causing Fer-1-insensitive death at higher concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B demonstrates narrow window of Fer-1-suppressible death.

claim: Sorafenib appears to trigger additional lethal mechanisms that act in parallel to the ferroptotic response at higher concentrations.
source: Thus, while sorafenib can inhibit system xc− activity robustly, this manifests as a ferroptotic cell death phenotype only over a narrow range of concentrations; sorafenib appears to trigger additional lethal mechanisms that act in parallel to the ferroptotic response at higher concentrations.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation of Fer-1-insensitive death at higher sorafenib concentrations.

claim: Nilotinib, masitinib, and imatinib do not trigger ferroptosis.
source: The global pattern of kinase inhibition by sorafenib against 300 purified kinase domains is highly similar to that of nilotinib, masitinib, and imatinib (Anastassiadis et al., 2011), yet none of these agents appear to trigger ferroptosis, as defined by sensitivity to ferroptosis-specific cell death inhibitors β-ME and Fer-1 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 5G demonstrates lack of β-ME and Fer-1 rescue for these compounds.

claim: Two lethal sorafenib analogs (SRS13-45 and SRS13-60) significantly inhibit glutamate release.
source: Consistent with the above data, two lethal sorafenib analogs (SRS13-45 and SRS13-60) significantly inhibited glutamate release, while two non-lethal analogs (EC50 >40 μM), SRS13-67 and SRS14-98, did not (Figure 6C).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 6C demonstrates inhibition by lethal analogs.

claim: Two non-lethal sorafenib analogs (SRS13-67 and SRS14-98) do not inhibit glutamate release.
source: Consistent with the above data, two lethal sorafenib analogs (SRS13-45 and SRS13-60) significantly inhibited glutamate release, while two non-lethal analogs (EC50 >40 μM), SRS13-67 and SRS14-98, did not (Figure 6C).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 6C demonstrates no inhibition by non-lethal analogs.

claim: The ability of sorafenib analogs to induce caspase-3/7 (DEVDase) activity does not vary significantly from one another or from DMSO-treated controls.
source: The ability of these analogs to induce caspase-3/7 (DEVDase) activity did not vary significantly from one another or from DMSO-treated controls, as compared to cells treated with a positive control inducer of apoptosis, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Caspase-3/7 activity assay data shown in Figure 6D demonstrates no significant induction by sorafenib analogs.

claim: Sorafenib treatment is associated with a significant number of adverse events in 15/20 physiological system categories, the most observed for any drug.
source: In this analysis, we observed that sorafenib treatment was associated with a significant number of adverse events in 15/20 physiological system categories, the most observed for any drug.
evidence: Analysis of FAERS data shown in Figure 7 demonstrates unique adverse event profile for sorafenib.

claim: Adverse events uniquely associated with sorafenib compared to all other kinase inhibitor drugs include musculoskeletal, nervous system, and pathological disorders as well as hemorrhage.
source: A subset of the adverse events uniquely associated with sorafenib compared to all other kinase inhibitor drugs included musculoskeletal, nervous system, and pathological disorders as well as hemorrhage
evidence: Analysis of FAERS data shown in Figure 7 demonstrates unique adverse events for sorafenib.

claim: Compared to other clinically-approved kinase inhibitors, sorafenib treatment has an increased propensity to generate unexpected adverse events in a variety of physiological systems.
source: These results suggest that, compared to other clinically-approved kinase inhibitors, sorafenib treatment has an increased propensity to generate unexpected adverse events in a variety of physiological systems.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the analysis of FAERS data showing unique adverse event patterns for sorafenib.

claim: Five clonal cell lines isolated from DU-145 cells display significant (>threefold) resistance to the lethal effects of erastin but not Taxol.
source: First, we isolated from DU-145 prostate cancer cells five clonal cell lines that displayed significant (>threefold) resistance to the lethal effects of erastin but not the multidrug resistance pump substrate Taxol (paclitaxel) (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 8B,C demonstrates selective resistance to erastin.

claim: Five erastin-resistant cell lines display significant resistance to SAS, sorafenib and more potent erastin analogs (20–22).
source: These five resistant cell lines displayed significant resistance to additional ferroptosis inducers including SAS, sorafenib and the more potent erastin analogs identified above (20–22) (Figure 8D,E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 8D,E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrates cross-resistance.

claim: Erastin-resistant cell lines display resistance to RSL3.
source: These lines also displayed resistance to RSL3, which triggers ferroptosis not through inhibition of system xc− but through the inhibition of the glutathione peroxidase GPX4 (Yang et al., 2014; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell viability data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrates resistance to RSL3.

claim: System xc− is equally sensitive to the inhibitory effects of erastin in the parental DU-145 line and the five resistant cell lines.
source: Indeed, using the glutamate release assay, we found that system xc− was equally sensitive to the inhibitory effects of erastin in the parental DU-145 line and the five resistant cell lines (Figure 8F).
evidence: Glutamate release assay data shown in Figure 8F demonstrates equivalent inhibition in resistant lines.

claim: The parental and resistant cell lines exhibit largely equivalent levels of basal total glutathione and depletion of glutathione following erastin treatment.
source: Likewise, the parental and resistant cell lines exhibited largely equivalent levels of basal total glutathione and depletion of glutathione following erastin treatment (Figure 8G).
evidence: Glutathione assay data shown in Figure 8G demonstrates equivalent glutathione levels and depletion.

claim: Erastin-resistant cell lines exhibit substantially lower levels of basal and erastin-induced ROS accumulation compared to parental DU-145 cells.
source: We observed that the resistant cell lines exhibited substantially lower levels of basal and erastin-induced ROS accumulation, as detected by H2DCFDA using flow cytometry (Figure 8H).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8H demonstrates reduced ROS accumulation in resistant lines.

claim: Resistance to various ferroptosis inducers is likely due to an inhibition of the accumulation of lethal oxidative species.
source: This result suggested that resistance to various ferroptosis inducers was likely due to an inhibition of the accumulation of lethal oxidative species.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation of reduced ROS accumulation in resistant cell lines.

claim: AKR1C1 is upregulated 586-fold in erastin-resistant cell lines compared to parental DU-145 cells.
source: The two genes that exhibited the highest average fold-change in expression and that were upregulated to highest average absolute levels within the cell (e.g., FPKM >100) were AKR1C1 (586-fold up-regulation) and AKR1C2 (528-fold up-regulation) (Figure 8I).
evidence: RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8I demonstrates 586-fold upregulation of AKR1C1.

claim: AKR1C2 is upregulated 528-fold in erastin-resistant cell lines compared to parental DU-145 cells.
source: The two genes that exhibited the highest average fold-change in expression and that were upregulated to highest average absolute levels within the cell (e.g., FPKM >100) were AKR1C1 (586-fold up-regulation) and AKR1C2 (528-fold up-regulation) (Figure 8I).
evidence: RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8I demonstrates 528-fold upregulation of AKR1C2.

claim: AKR1C3 is upregulated 84-fold in erastin-resistant cell lines compared to parental DU-145 cells.
source: A third family member, AKR1C3 was upregulated 84-fold.
evidence: RNA-Seq data demonstrates 84-fold upregulation of AKR1C3.

claim: AKR1C1-3 enzymes participate in the detoxification of toxic lipid metabolites (such as 4-hydroxynonenal) generated downstream of the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid species.
source: The AKR1C1-3 enzymes have been shown to participate in the detoxification of toxic lipid metabolites (such as 4-hydroxynonenal) generated downsteam of the oxidation of various polyunsaturated fatty acid species (Figure 8J; Burczynski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on AKR1C enzyme function.

claim: Overexpression of AKR1C family members may confer partial resistance to erastin by enhancing the detoxification of reactive aldehydes generated downstream of the oxidative destruction of the plasma membrane during ferroptosis.
source: Thus, overexpression of AKR1C family members (and potentially other genes) may confer partial resistance to erastin by enhancing the detoxification of reactive aldehydes generated downstream of the oxidative destruction of the plasma membrane during ferroptosis.
evidence: This hypothesis is based on the known function of AKR1C enzymes and their dramatic upregulation in resistant cells.

claim: Erastin and SAS trigger ferroptosis in human HT-1080 fibrosarcoma cells grown on two-dimensional substrates with atmospheric levels of oxygen (21% oxygen).
source: Erastin and SAS were previously shown to trigger ferroptosis in human HT-1080 fibrosarcoma cells grown on two-dimensional substrates with atmospheric levels of oxygen (i.e., 21% oxygen) (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RSL3 triggers ferroptosis by inhibiting GPX4.
source: For comparison, we also tested the growth inhibitory effects of (1S, 3R)-RSL3 (hereafter RSL3), a small molecule that triggers ferroptosis by inhibiting GPX4, which is downstream of system xc− in the ferroptotic cascade (Yang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: β-ME treatment can generate mixed disulfides taken up by other transporters, thereby circumventing the need for system xc− function.
source: The inhibition of cell death by β-ME indicates that cell death most likely involves inhibition of system xc− function, as β-ME treatment can generate mixed disulfides taken up by other transporters, thereby circumventing the need for system xc− function (Ishii et al., 1981).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At clinically recommended doses (400 mg), it is possible to achieve maximum plasma concentration of sorafenib from 5.2–21 μM.
source: Data collected in Phase I clinical trials of sorafenib-treated patients demonstrate that at clinically recommended doses (400 mg), it is possible to achieve maximum plasma concentration of sorafenib from 5.2–21 μM (Awada et al., 2005; Strumberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial data.

claim: Sera collected from sorafenib-treated patients display evidence of protein oxidation, with higher levels of protein oxidation being correlated with improved patient outcomes.
source: Notably, sera collected from sorafenib-treated patients display evidence of protein oxidation, with higher levels of protein oxidation being correlated with improved patient outcomes (Coriat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous clinical research.

claim: Renal cell carcinomas are among the most sensitive of all cancer cell lines to the lethal effects of erastin.
source: Indeed, given that renal cell carcinomas are among the most sensitive of all cancer cell lines to the lethal effects of erastin (Yang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The expression of AKR1C genes is controlled by the antioxidant master regulatory transcription factor NRF2, which itself is under the negative regulation of KEAP1.
source: The expression of the AKR1C genes is controlled by the antioxidant master regulatory transcription factor NRF2, which itself is under the negative regulation of KEAP1 (Lou et al., 2006; Agyeman et al., 2012; Jung and Kwak, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on gene regulation.

claim: Mutations of NRF2 and KEAP1 are observed in numerous cancers.
source: Mutations of both these genes are observed in numerous cancers (Jaramillo and Zhang, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations in NRF2 and KEAP1 may enhance AKR1C expression and possibly render cells resistant to the induction of ferroptosis downstream of system xc− inhibition.
source: and we would predict that these changes enhance AKR1C expression and possibly render cells resistant to the induction of ferroptosis downstream of system xc− inhibition.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known regulatory relationships and observed resistance mechanisms.

claim: In cells lacking system xc−, erastin can inhibit structurally-related transporters (e.g., system L).
source: Further, given evidence that Jurkat cells do not express system xc− (Kakazu et al., 2011), we hypothesize that in cells lacking system xc−, erastin can inhibit structurally-related transporters (e.g., system L).
evidence: This hypothesis is based on previous observations in Jurkat cells and a citation about system xc− expression.

claim: Erastin may bind to some indirect target that, in different cell types, favors the inhibition of different transporters.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that erastin binds to some indirect target that, in Jurkat cells, favors the inhibition of system L, while in HT-1080, Calu-1 and possibly other cells, favors the inhibition of system xc−.
evidence: This is presented as an alternative hypothesis to explain differential transporter inhibition.

claim: System xc− inhibitors may further reduce cell growth or cause cell death by restricting the intracellular supply of cysteine and inhibiting new protein synthesis.
source: However, these compounds are also predicted to inactivate the cystine/cysteine redox cycle (Banjac et al., 2008) and, by restricting the intracellular supply of cysteine, to inhibit new protein synthesis. Together, these effects may further reduce cell growth or cause cell death in certain contexts where the induction of ferroptosis per se is not possible.
evidence: This is a prediction based on known effects of cysteine depletion and a citation.

claim: ATF4 is an important regulator of SLC7A11 expression.
source: Intriguingly, ATF4 is thought to be an important regulator of SLC7A11 expression and deletion of Atf4 in mouse embryonic fibroblast cells results in an oxidative, iron-dependent death phenotype that is highly reminiscent of ferroptosis (Harding et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Deletion of Atf4 in mouse embryonic fibroblast cells results in an oxidative, iron-dependent death phenotype that is highly reminiscent of ferroptosis.
source: Intriguingly, ATF4 is thought to be an important regulator of SLC7A11 expression and deletion of Atf4 in mouse embryonic fibroblast cells results in an oxidative, iron-dependent death phenotype that is highly reminiscent of ferroptosis (Harding et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The basal level of ATF4 may set the threshold for ferroptotic death.
source: suggesting that the basal level of ATF4 may set the threshold for ferroptotic death.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the known role of ATF4 in regulating SLC7A11 and the death phenotype observed with Atf4 deletion.

claim: ChaC-family proteins function in yeast as intracellular glutathione-degrading enzymes.
source: ChaC-family proteins were recently reported to function in yeast as intracellular glutathione-degrading enzymes (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CHAC1 upregulation following system xc− inhibition may actively contribute to glutathione depletion in cells deprived of cysteine.
source: One possibility is that CHAC1 upregulation following system xc− inhibition may actively contribute to glutathione depletion in cells deprived of cysteine, although inhibition of CHAC1 transcription had only minimal effects on the viability of erastin-treated cells.
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on known CHAC1 function, though experimental data suggests minimal effect on viability.

claim: Sorafenib treatment inhibits translation.
source: It has previously been shown that sorafenib treatment inhibits translation (Rahmani et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sorafenib induces ER stress and the expression of DDIT4 (REDD1) via the eIF2alpha-ATF4 pathway.
source: induces ER stress and the expression of DDIT4 (REDD1) via the eIF2alpha-ATF4 pathway (Rahmani et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sorafenib causes caspase-independent death.
source: and causes caspase-independent death (Panka et al., 2006; Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In hepatocellular carcinoma cells, sorafenib can trigger iron-dependent death.
source: Most recently, it was suggested that in hepatocellular carcinoma cells, sorafenib can trigger iron-dependent death (Louandre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The efficacy of sorafenib observed in patients could be due, at least in part, to inhibition of system xc−-mediated cystine uptake.
source: Indeed, given that renal cell carcinomas are among the most sensitive of all cancer cell lines to the lethal effects of erastin (Yang et al., 2014), it may be of interest to re-evaluate whether the efficacy of sorafenib observed in patients could be due, at least in part, to inhibition of system xc−-mediated cystine uptake.
evidence: This is presented as a speculation based on the sensitivity of renal cell carcinomas to erastin and sorafenib's ability to inhibit system xc−.

claim: Specific underlying sensitizing factors will render a minority of individuals more sensitive to sorafenib adverse events.
source: While not all patients treated with sorafenib experience adverse events, we suspect that specific underlying (and unknown) sensitizing factors will render a minority of individuals more sensitive to these events.
evidence: This is presented as a speculation to explain the variable occurrence of adverse events.
